title: Medieval music
description: Western music created during the Middle Ages
wiki_lead:
Medieval music encompasses the sacred and secular music of Western Europe during the Middle Ages, from approximately the 6th to 15th centuries. It is the first and longest major era of Western classical music and is followed by the Renaissance music; the two eras comprise what musicologists generally term as early music, preceding the common practice period. Following the traditional division of the Middle Ages, medieval music can be divided into Early (500–1150), High (1150–1300), and Late (1300–1400) medieval music.
Medieval music includes liturgical music used for the church, other sacred music, and secular or non-religious music. Much medieval music is purely vocal music, such as Gregorian chant. Other music used only instruments or both voices and instruments (typically with the instruments accompanying the voices). 
The medieval period saw the creation and adaptation of systems of music notation which enabled creators to document and transmit musical ideas more easily, although notation coexisted with and complemented oral tradition.

It is the first and longest major era of Western classical music and is followed by the Renaissance music; the two eras comprise what musicologists generally term as early music, preceding the common practice period. Following the traditional division of the Middle Ages, medieval music can be divided into Early (500–1150), High (1150–1300), and Late (1300–1400) medieval music.

Other music used only instruments or both voices and instruments (typically with the instruments accompanying the voices). 
The medieval period saw the creation and adaptation of systems of music notation which enabled creators to document and transmit musical ideas more easily, although notation coexisted with and complemented oral tradition.


Background


Origins


Greco-Roman
De Institutione Musica (c. 510) by Boethius (480–524) taught the medievals ancient Greek and Roman music, such as Pythagorean tuning.


Christian

The fall of Rome (c. 476) also saw the rise of Christianity, after the conversion of emperor Constantine the Great (272–337).
Christians versed in the Bible attributed the invention of music to Jubal, "the father of all who play stringed instruments and pipes" in Genesis 4:21. Horns are added when God commands Moses to forge two silver trumpets in  Numbers 10:2. Jubal's half-brother, the first smith Tubal-cain, is also given the title of inventor of music, from copying errors, and a Christian retelling of the story of Pythagorean hammers.
King David's retinue with the Ark of the Covenant includes Heman and Jeduthun, who 1 Chronicles 16:42 states "were responsible for the sounding of the trumpets and cymbals and for the playing of the other instruments for sacred song." In 1 Chronicles 25:1: "David, together with the commanders of the army, set apart some of the sons of Asaph, Heman and Jeduthun for the ministry of prophesying, accompanied by harps, lyres and cymbals." The Psalms are attributed to them.
Hilary of Poitiers (c. 310–c. 367) and Saint Ambrose of Milan (c. 339–397) were pioneers of Latin hymns. Isidore of Seville (c. 560–636), described by historian Charles Forbes René de Montalembert (1810–1870), as "the last scholar of the ancient world", also wrote extensively on music.


Instruments

As well as singing, many instruments used to perform medieval music still exist today, but in different and typically more technologically developed forms.


Brass
There were medieval brass horns or trumpets such as the buisine and arguably slide trumpet precursors to the modern trombone (called the sackbut).


Woodwind
The flute was made of wood in the medieval era rather than silver or other metal, and could be made as a side-blown or end-blown instrument (e. g. tibia). While modern orchestral flutes are usually made of metal and have complex key mechanisms and airtight pads, medieval flutes had holes that the performer had to cover with the fingers (as with the recorder). The recorder was made of wood during the medieval era rather than synthetic materials such as plastic, it has more or less retained its past form. 
The gemshorn is similar to the recorder as it has finger holes on its front, though it is actually a member of the ocarina family. One of the flute's predecessors, the pan flute, was popular in medieval times, and is possibly of Hellenic origin. This instrument's pipes were made of wood, and were graduated in length to produce different pitches.
Early versions of the pipe organ such as the water organ also existed. In 666, Pope Vitalian introduced the organ in Rome. In 757, Byzantine emperor Constantine V (718–775) sent an organ as a gift to Carolingian King of the Franks Pippin the Short (c. 714–768)
grok_lead: Medieval music refers to the Western European musical traditions spanning approximately 500 to 1400 CE, a vast era that bridges the fall of the Roman Empire and the dawn of the Renaissance, characterized by its deep ties to the Christian liturgy and the emergence of both sacred and secular forms. The period's sacred music was dominated by Gregorian chant, a monophonic, unaccompanied vocal repertoire developed during the Carolingian Renaissance through the fusion of Roman and Gallican traditions, serving as the primary music for Catholic worship in monasteries and cathedrals. This chant, named after Pope Gregory I (c. 540â604) though compiled later, emphasized modal scales, Latin texts from the Bible and liturgy, and expressive melodies without strict metrical rhythm. From the 9th century onward, early experiments in polyphony appeared, with organum adding a second voice in parallel intervals to the chant line, evolving into more elaborate forms at the Notre Dame School in Paris during the 12th century under composers like LÃ©onin and PÃ©rotin, who introduced rhythmic modes and multi-voice textures. By the 14th century, the Ars Nova movement, particularly in France and Italy, refined polyphony with isorhythmic structures, duple meter, and greater rhythmic complexity, as seen in the works of Guillaume de Machaut. Secular music flourished alongside sacred traditions, notably through the songs of troubadours in southern France (writing in Occitan) and trouvÃ¨res in the north (in Old French), who composed courtly love lyrics (cansos) on themes of chivalry, romance, and politics, often performed by jongleurs or minstrels with lute or vielle accompaniment. These vernacular traditions, peaking in the 12th and 13th centuries, contrasted with the Latin dominance of church music and reflected the cultural vibrancy of feudal courts. Key figures include Hildegard von Bingen (1098â1179), a Benedictine abbess whose visionary monophonic chants and moral plays like Ordo Virtutum blend mysticism and music, and Guillaume de Machaut (c. 1300â1377), the era's most prominent composer, celebrated for his polyphonic Messe de Nostre Dame âthe first complete setting of the Ordinary by a single composerâand intricate motets. Other notables encompass PÃ©rotin (fl. c. 1200), innovator of four-voice polyphony, and Italian trecento composers like Francesco Landini (c. 1325â1397), known for ballate blending sacred and secular influences. Musical notation advanced significantly, beginning with neumes in the 9th century âsimple symbols indicating pitch contours and groups of notes (melismas) sung to a single syllable, but lacking precise rhythm âand progressing to mensural notation by the 13th century, pioneered by Franco of Cologne, which specified durations through note shapes and ligatures, enabling the notated preservation of complex polyphony. Instruments such as the organ, harp, and fiddle supported vocal performance but were secondary, with music theory drawing from Boethius's ancient concepts of musica speculativa (speculative music) and practical treatises like those of Guido d'Arezzo (c. 991â1033), who introduced the solmization syllables (ut, re, mi). Overall, medieval music's innovationsâfrom chant's meditative purity to polyphony's layered harmonies and secular poetry's emotional depthâestablished core elements of Western musical structure, notation, and performance that influenced subsequent eras.
